result.summary: Mercury leads the suitors' ghosts to Hades, where Agamemnon and Achilles speak of Achilles' funeral and Amphimedon tells how the suitors died. Ulysses then finds his father Laertes on his farm, tests and reveals himself to him, and the Ithacans, led by Eupeithes, march against them until Minerva and Jove impose peace.

scenes.title: Mercury leads the suitors' ghosts
scenes.summary: Mercury guides the whining ghosts of the suitors down to the meadow of asphodel, where they find Achilles, Agamemnon and other heroes.

scenes.title: Achilles and Agamemnon compare deaths
scenes.summary: Achilles laments Agamemnon's miserable death; Agamemnon recalls Achilles' glorious death, mourning and funeral at Troy.

scenes.title: Amphimedon tells of the slaughter
scenes.summary: Agamemnon questions Amphimedon, who recounts Penelope's web, Ulysses' return and the killing of the suitors. Agamemnon praises Penelope and condemns Clytemnestra.

scenes.title: Ulysses reveals himself to Laertes
scenes.summary: Ulysses finds his father hoeing, tests him with a false tale, then proves his identity with his scar and the trees.
scenes.stakes: Laertes' grief and Ulysses' wish to be recognised by his father.

scenes.title: Dinner at Laertes' house
scenes.summary: Minerva rejuvenates Laertes, and Dolius and his sons joyfully greet Ulysses at dinner.

scenes.title: The assembly of Ithaca
scenes.summary: Rumour spreads, the dead are buried, and Eupeithes urges revenge. Medon and Halitherses counsel peace, but most follow Eupeithes to arms.
scenes.stakes: The Ithacans risk civil war and Eupeithes' death in pursuing revenge.

scenes.title: Minerva and Jove decide on peace
scenes.summary: Minerva asks Jove his plan; he tells her to make peace with Ulysses ruling.

scenes.title: Battle and peace
scenes.summary: Ulysses' band arms and meets the Ithacans; Laertes kills Eupeithes. Minerva halts the fighting and makes a covenant of peace.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses and his small band face the whole angry town, and Jove's anger.

notable_quotes.reason: Agamemnon predicts Penelope's lasting fame for constancy.
Agamemnon says Achilles' fame survives death.

analysis.text: The book closes the epic with reunion, recognition and restored order, contrasting Penelope's loyalty with Clytemnestra's betrayal.
The ending shows heroic values of kleos, blood vengeance, and the need for divine intervention to stop cycles of revenge.

legacy.text: Ancient scholars debated whether Book 24 was authentic; Aristarchus is said to have marked the Odyssey's true end at Book 23.

fun_facts.text: The scene of Ulysses proving himself by naming the trees echoes Penelope's bed test in Book 23.

language_notes.text: "Mercury of Cyllene": Mercury (the Greek Hermes) is named for Mount Cyllene in Arcadia, his legendary birthplace. His wand puts men to sleep or wakes them.
Asphodel is a pale wild lily-like plant; in Homer its meadow is where the undistinguished dead dwell.
"Danaans" is one of Homer's names for the Greeks, as are Achaeans and Argives, used interchangeably in this passage.
"All huge and hugely" echoes Homer's line describing Achilles' enormous body sprawled in the dust, with his skill in chariot-driving forgotten.
"The old man of the sea" is the sea god Nereus; his daughters, the Nereids, include Thetis, Achilles' mother.
"Dirge" is a funeral song of mourning; "chaunted" is an old spelling of chanted.
Bacchus (the Greek Dionysus) gave the vase, and Vulcan (Hephaestus), god of the forge, made it; Thetis brought it for Achilles' bones.
Mercury (the Greek Hermes) guides the dead to the underworld, which is why he leads the suitors' ghosts here.
"Cattle-lifting" means raiding and stealing cattle, a common form of plunder in the heroic world.
A tambour frame is a round embroidery frame holding cloth taut; the term is anachronistic, used by the translator for Penelope's loom.
A pall is a funeral cloth, here a shroud to cover a dead body.
"In the waning of moons" means as months passed. The 186 is a footnote marker, not part of the story.
The contest of the bow and iron (axe heads) was set by Penelope; the arrow had to pass through them.
"Cloister" here means the pillared court or hall of the house, not a monastery.
The daughter of Tyndareus is Clytemnestra, who with her lover killed Agamemnon on his return from Troy.
A lean-to is a shed with a sloping roof built against the main wall. A Sicel is a person from Sicily.
"Make trial of" means to test. Ulysses wants to put his father to the proof before revealing himself.
"Unsavoury" here means unwashed and unpleasant to be near, not morally bad.
Eperitus is a false name, and the Alybas and Apheidas details are part of Ulysses' invented story.
Birds on the right were a favourable omen. Reading flight patterns was a common Greek way to predict outcomes.
Pouring dust on the head was an ancient gesture of deep grief and mourning.
The scar comes from a boar hunt on Mt. Parnassus, an event Ulysses recalls as proof. The same scar identified him to his nurse Euryclea earlier.
Olympus was the home of the gods. Laertes takes the suitors' punishment as proof that the gods still watch over justice.
A Sicel is a woman from Sicily; she is Dolius' wife and serves as Laertes' attendant, as sentence 128 explains.
"Would, by Father Jove..." is an archaic wish meaning "I wish to Jove, Minerva and Apollo"; it introduces an unfulfilled desire to be young again.
Laertes recalls capturing Nericum, a coastal stronghold, when he ruled the Cephallenians, the people of Ulysses' kingdom around Ithaca.
Kissing the hand "at the wrist" is a gesture of respectful affection from a servant to his master.
"All hail" is an old greeting of welcome. The number 187 is a stray footnote marker from the edition, not part of the speech.
Rumour is personified as a messenger spreading news;
Cephallenians is the name used for Ulysses' subjects, the island peoples of his kingdom including Ithaca.
Pylos (Nestor's city) and Elis (home of the Epeans) lie on the Greek mainland, the likely places for Ulysses to flee.
"Knew both past and future" means Halitherses was a seer who read omens, as he did earlier in the poem.
"Wantonness" means reckless, unrestrained insolence; "substance" means wealth and property.
"Son of Saturn" is Jove's regular title; Saturn was the older god whom Jove overthrew. "King of kings" marks his supremacy among the gods.
"In virtue of which" means by the authority of which; the covenant is a sworn agreement that lets Ulysses keep ruling.
"Mettle" means courage and character, which a battle tests.
"Vying" means competing; Laertes delights that son and grandson compete in bravery.
"Blue-eyed damsel" is Minerva herself, addressed in the third person while she is disguised as Mentor; the Greek epithet is usually rendered "grey-eyed."
"Warful" is an archaic, unusual coinage meaning full of war.

context_notes.text: Mercury also served as guide of souls to the underworld, which is why he leads the suitors' ghosts here.
A mound over one's ashes was the honour owed to a fallen warrior, ensuring lasting fame for him and his son.
Agamemnon was murdered on his return from Troy by Aegisthus and his own wife Clytemnestra, who had taken Aegisthus as lover.
Amphimedon was one of the suitors. Agamemnon had earlier visited Ithaca and been his host, so guest-friendship binds them.
Agamemnon and his brother Menelaus gathered heroes for the Trojan war; Ulysses was reluctant to go, according to tradition.
Penelope's faithfulness is contrasted with Clytemnestra's betrayal, a central contrast in the poem.
Laertes is Ulysses' aged father. He has withdrawn to a country farm, grieving, since his son's long absence.
A talent was a measure of weight, used for gold and silver. Seven talents would be a very large gift.
Laertes fears revenge from the suitors' kinsmen in Ithaca and the nearby Cephallenian lands, which Ulysses ruled.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) is Ulysses' divine protector and often alters mortals' appearance to help him.
Dolius is Laertes' old servant, who tends his orchard and farm. His sons work with him.
Antinous was the leading suitor and the first killed by Ulysses, shot through the throat with an arrow while drinking.
Medon was the herald and Phemius the bard; both were spared by Ulysses because they had served the suitors only under compulsion.
The god was Minerva, who had taken Mentor's form during the fight in the hall.
Laertes is Ulysses' aged father; Dolius is an old servant who farms Laertes' land. Both fight despite their age.
Mentor is an Ithacan friend of Ulysses' household. Minerva often takes his shape to guide and aid Ulysses and Telemachus.
Eupeithes is the father of the suitor Antinous and leads the avengers' relatives against Ulysses.

literary_notes.text: The suitors' ghosts are compared to squealing bats in a cave, conveying their eerie, pitiful and animal-like noise.
Agamemnon calls Achilles happy for dying gloriously in battle, setting up the contrast with his own shameful death at home.
Clashing armour, resin, honey and the tramp of a multitude create a vivid sensory picture of the funeral pyre.
Enduring fame after death (kleos) is the central heroic value; Achilles' name outlives his body.
The great king appears as a beggar, so the suitors mock the very man who will destroy them.
"The ground seethed with our blood" compares spilled blood to boiling liquid, making the slaughter vivid and horrible.
Agamemnon predicts that songs will celebrate Penelope, as the Odyssey itself does.
Agamemnon sets Clytemnestra's hateful song against Penelope's glorious one, sharpening the contrast between the two wives.
The detailed picture of patched shirt, leg thongs and goat skin cap shows Laertes' sorrowful self-neglect and prepares the reader's pity.
Ulysses' choice to be crafty shows his habit of testing and deceiving even loved ones, his defining trait.
Laertes praises the hospitality of his own son to a stranger, not knowing the stranger is that son.
Grief is described as a dark cloud falling upon Laertes, making his sorrow tangible.
The trees recall the recurring Odyssey motif of proofs of identity, here tied to home, family and memory.
Telemachus' comparison of his father to an immortal shows how striking Minerva's transformation is.
Laertes imagines how he would have fought the suitors, though they are already dead; his regret comes too late.
Ulysses' good-natured scolding shows him relaxed and warm after the slaughter, treating his servants as familiar friends.
Rumour is treated as a figure who travels through the town, making the speed of news seem like a living force.
Halitherses blames the people's own failure to restrain the suitors, while they now prepare another act of folly.
The narrator announces Eupeithes' death in advance, undercutting his hope of vengeance and signalling the coming battle.
Jove reminds Minerva that she herself arranged Ulysses' return, gently showing the gods' plan is already settled.
Ulysses is compared to a soaring eagle swooping on prey, conveying his speed, power and fierce renewed energy.
Jove's thunderbolt lands before Minerva, a sign of divine authority that ends the human conflict.
